newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels seize northeast Zairean town, gold mines.
newsitem.headline: Rebels seize northeast Zairean town, gold mines.

text.p: Rebels seized the strategic northeastern Zaire town of Bunia and nearby gold mines in a fierce battle with government forces which left hundreds dead, residents said on Thursday.
"The fighting was terrible and there were bodies all over the streets, those of us who had not already fled to the forest had to stay in our homes," said teacher Pierre Lolo.
"We are only glad it is quiet now and the army has gone. They can never come back here."
Bunia fell to rebels trying to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko after a 12-hour battle on December 24. Rebels say 307 government soldiers were killed while their own forces sustained 75 casualties.

Bunia resident Tonalumozi Selenge said townspeople had buried the bodies of 242 people -- all but two of them fighters -- killed on December 24. He said wounded from the battle were still in Bunia's hospital, which was running short of medicine.
Bunia was the greatest strategic advance made by Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces in several weeks, with its all-weather airport and significant nearby gold reserves.
Residents confirmed rebel claims the Kilo-Moto gold mining area 80-km (50-miles) from Bunia was captured by the rebels.

Regional Commissioner Mbembe Ndoy, who worked for Zaire's government but defected to the rebels when they seized Bunia, said Kimin gold mine, believed to be the largest in the area, was looted by Zairean troops.

"The workers have all fled but the houses have been looted. Clearly a lot of equipment was stolen but we believe the processing plant is intact," said Mbembe, adding his information came from people who fled the area during the rebel advance.

The Kimin mine is in a 2,000-square-km (772-square-mile) concession granted by Okimo (Office des Mines d'Or de Kilo-Moto) to a Canadian-Belgium consortium. The Okimo concession covers a total of 83,000-square-km (32,000-square-miles) around Bunia.

"The mine has been secured but the enemy is still around in the bush and it is not yet safe for civilians to go there," said rebel officer Bernard Wandera, who would not allow a Reuters reporter to travel to Kimin.
Last month Kabila ordered gold miners, including foreign holders of concessions, to come forward and discuss the future of their operations by January 3 or risk losing their assets.
With the capture of Bunia the rebels hold a swathe over 600 -km (400-miles) long bordering on Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
The rebels hope to use income from Zairean minerals and commodities like coffee to fund their rebellion.
The fighting in Bunia was heaviest around the airport. The town centre bears the ravages of systematic looting over a period of three weeks.
Small groups of people drift quietly along the dusty main street, picking up what they can salvage or just looking and glad to be still alive.
Everything of value which could be carried away has gone.
Windows are smashed and doors hang loose on their hinges. Some shops were torched before the army left and the soot-blackened shells stand out like rotten teeth.

"The soldiers began looting on December 2, and that was when many people ran away, then they started to accuse us of being rebels and if they caught more than five people together they were immediately accused," said businessman Emmanuel Mambala.
"If you couldn't pay them then you would be killed, and many people were."
